title: Local Calibration of APT Data Scaling for Diffusion Calculations
content: Diffusion is a foundational atomic-level phenomenon that strongly affects how materials perform and evolve in a variety of environments. In metals, mass transport is associated with phase transformations, the degradation of alloys in corrosive or oxidative environments, and radiation-induced segregation or embrittlement in nuclear environments. On the other hand, ionic transport drives the functional properties of battery and other energy storage or generation schemes, providing an essential positive benefit. Quantification of diffusion is therefore of significant interest in a variety of scientific communities. Measurements of diffusion have oftentimes relied on isotopic tracers whose distributions can be intentionally introduced and monitored as external stimuli (temperature, radiation, chemical gradients) are applied to redistribute the isotopes. The evolution of these isotopic distributions can then be fitted to models of diffusion to derive quantitative measures of diffusion, energy barriers, and the potential of the external stimuli to alter atomic transport. Various microscopy techniques have been used to measure isotopic redistributions. Mass spectrometry-based methods have been broadly used to measured stable or radioactive isotopic tracers. Secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) is perhaps the most widely used method for these studies and has been tremendously successful in quantifying thermal diffusion and accelerated diffusion in a variety of systems [1]. While SIMS has a depth resolution approaching the nanometer scale and excellent isotopic sensitivity, its reliance on relatively large sputter areas (10s to 100s of micrometers) can obscure subtle or heterogenous differences in local isotopic profiles.
